clue.text: Lions meet by arrangement for big event

indicators.note: things put in an arrangement are set out in a new order, so the preceding words get reordered

parts.note: the two words taken letter for letter as fodder

explanation.surface: A pride of lions gathering in formation would be quite an occasion on the savannah.
explanation.definitionFit: A milestone is a significant event or stage in a life or project, so a big event in figurative terms.

clue.text: Marriage is a contest

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a pairing of two people, as when a good couple is called a fine one
second meaning: a game or sporting fixture between opponents

explanation.surface: A cynical quip that married life is a constant battle.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a union of partners and a sporting fixture such as a football game.

clue.text: Wild one, knocked about, to take easy

indicators.note: something knocked about is battered out of shape, so its letters are jumbled

parts.note: the two words used letter for letter as fodder

explanation.surface: A rowdy character, roughed up in a scuffle, needs to rest and recover.
explanation.definitionFit: To recline on a bed or sofa is to rest, which is taking things easy.

clue.text: Catch sight of jumpers and blouses being pulled up

indicators.note: in a down clue, pulling a word up means reading it from the bottom, that is backwards

parts.note: jumpers and blouses are both garments for the upper body

explanation.surface: Someone notices clothing being hauled upward, perhaps on a washing line.
explanation.definitionFit: To spot something is to notice or glimpse it, a plain verb synonym for seeing it suddenly.

clue.text: Egg-shaped ring given to Valery

parts.note: a ring is round like the letter O
Val is the usual short form of the name Valery; that the letters also run across 'to Valery' is a coincidence

explanation.surface: An oddly shaped ring is presented as a gift to someone called Valery.
explanation.walkthrough: The name is cut to its familiar short form, as friends would call him or her.
explanation.definitionFit: Oval describes a rounded elongated outline like that of a hen's egg, from Latin ovum.

clue.text: Moving abroad, but eccentric GI to remain

indicators.note: eccentric means off-centre or odd, so the letters that follow are put in an odd order

parts.note: all the letters of these three words form the fodder

explanation.surface: An American soldier stationed overseas decides, unusually, to settle there instead of going home.
explanation.walkthrough: A GI is an American soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: Emigration is leaving your own country to settle in another, a noun for relocating overseas.

clue.text: Count is first person to break foot

indicators.note: breaking into something means getting inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: the foot of something is its base
the first-person pronoun

explanation.surface: Reads like arithmetic or a grammar lesson about first persons and feet.
explanation.walkthrough: Count is a title, not a verb: Count Basie was the American jazz pianist and bandleader.
explanation.definitionFit: William 'Count' Basie, swing-era bandleader, so the title alone points to his surname.

clue.text: Live with Oscar, blushing and disoriented

parts.note: to be is to exist or live
Oscar Wilde, the Irish playwright
a blushing face turns this colour

explanation.surface: Sharing a home with Oscar leaves someone flushed and confused.
explanation.walkthrough: Oscar suggests the NATO alphabet's O, but here it is the famous wit.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone bewildered is confused and has lost their bearings, which is being disoriented.

clue.text: Dennis of Bolsover is a man to prepare hides

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the long-serving Labour MP for Bolsover in Derbyshire
second meaning: a worker who strips and treats animal pelts

explanation.surface: A politician is described as someone who works with animal hides.
explanation.walkthrough: Dennis Skinner was Labour MP for Bolsover, a Derbyshire constituency, from 1970 to 2019, nicknamed the Beast of Bolsover.
explanation.definitionFit: The MP's surname is also the trade name for one who removes and dresses animal pelts.

clue.text: Always the first woman to have a supporter

parts.note: in Genesis, the first woman created
a sloping roof beam that holds up the roof

explanation.surface: A suggestion that women have always needed someone backing them.
explanation.definitionFit: As in happily ever after: from then on for all time, an adverbial phrase for forever.

clue.text: Wilkie Collins's bride?

parts.note: surface reading: the woman the Victorian novelist married
setter's reading: a bride is traditionally dressed in a pale gown, and Collins wrote a famous novel with that description as its title

explanation.walkthrough: Collins never married; the question mark marks the joke that the title of his 1859 mystery novel describes any bride.
explanation.definitionFit: Collins's sensation novel bears this title, and a bride in her wedding dress fits the phrase literally.

clue.text: Covering a hole in the coal scuttle

indicators.note: one item sitting in another means it is placed inside it

parts.note: a hod is a coal scuttle as well as a builder's carrier
the letter O looks like a hole

explanation.surface: A cover is needed for a gap in the bucket holding coal.
explanation.definitionFit: A hood is a covering for the head or for machinery, such as a car bonnet.

clue.text: Repair ark with nails in this island country

indicators.note: repairing something means rebuilding it, so these letters are reassembled differently

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Instructions to fix up Noah's boat with nails in a particular island nation.
explanation.definitionFit: Sri Lanka is a nation occupying an island off the southern tip of India.

clue.text: Smash the glass — it is most hideous

indicators.note: smashing something breaks it into pieces, which are then put together in another order

parts.note: the words of the fodder taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Someone urges breaking a mirror or vase because it is so ugly.
explanation.definitionFit: Ghastly means horrible or very ugly, so its superlative is the most horrible of all.

clue.text: Troubled, but died keeping weight down

indicators.note: keeping something means holding it, so one word holds another inside it

parts.note: taken as written
stress is pressure or a load bearing downwards

explanation.surface: Someone was worried but passed away with their weight unaffected.
explanation.walkthrough: The inner word goes in after the first two letters of the outer one.
explanation.definitionFit: Distressed means anxious, upset or in difficulty, a direct synonym for troubled in mind.

clue.text: Nick's first to lose heart, being a miser

indicators.note: losing heart means the middle of the word drops out

parts.note: to nick and to pinch both mean to steal
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man called Nick is the first to give up hope, perhaps because he is mean.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick looks like a name but is the verb meaning steal. The middle letter R comes out of the second word.
explanation.definitionFit: A pinchfist is an old word for a stingy person, one who keeps a tight grip on money.

clue.text: Pa is in Paris, getting us put up together at the same time

indicators.note: one word being in another means it sits inside it

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting a word up means writing it bottom to top, so backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Father is visiting the French capital and puts the family up there.
explanation.walkthrough: The short word goes inside the city's name just before its final S; then the two-letter pronoun is added backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Pari passu is Latin for 'with equal step', used of things proceeding side by side or simultaneously.

clue.text: Wading bird: regret head not visible

indicators.note: with the head out of sight, the word loses its first letter

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A long-legged bird looks sorry for itself, hiding its face.
explanation.definitionFit: The egret is a white heron that feeds by wading in shallow water.

clue.text: One, taking part in darts, remains

indicators.note: taking part in something places one inside it, so one piece is put within another

parts.note: darts as a verb means dashes or runs
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone joining a game of darts in a pub somehow stays put.
explanation.walkthrough: Darts is not the pub game but a verb for quick dashes.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruins are what is left of a destroyed building, the remains of a structure.

clue.text: Guides to unite trendy daughter with former husbands

parts.note: fashionable things are said to be in
standard abbreviation for daughter
former partners are exes

explanation.surface: Advice manuals for bringing a fashionable girl together with her mother's ex-husbands.
explanation.definitionFit: Indexes point readers to topics in a book or show trends, so they serve as guides.

clue.text: Sprinkle toes with water, but not on this sofa!

indicators.note: sprinkling scatters things about, so these letters are scattered and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A warning to rinse your feet somewhere other than on the new settee.
explanation.definitionFit: A small couch built for a pair of people is sold as a two-seater.

clue.text: A strain remedied by a former Russian empress

indicators.note: something remedied has been put right, so the letters are put into a corrected order

parts.note: the two words used letter for letter

explanation.surface: A pulled muscle cured by a royal from imperial Russia.
explanation.definitionFit: A tsarina was the wife of a tsar or a ruling empress of pre-revolutionary Russia.

clue.text: Large lad in the sea turned and went by bike?

indicators.note: a thing turned round faces the other way, so the whole is read backwards
one thing in another means it is placed inside it

parts.note: the deep is a poetic term for the sea
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
taken as written

explanation.surface: A big boy goes swimming, turns round, then cycles off.
explanation.walkthrough: The pair of pieces goes inside the sea word after its first two letters; then everything is read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Pushing pedals is how you propel a bicycle; the question mark admits pedalling could drive other machines.

clue.text: "The End of the Affair" is unbiased

indicators.note: the end of a word is its tail, and the answer sits in those closing letters

parts.note: the closing letters of this word

explanation.surface: Quotes the title of a Graham Greene novel and pronounces it impartial.
explanation.walkthrough: The End of the Affair is a 1951 novel by Graham Greene; read literally, it points to the tail of its last word.
explanation.definitionFit: Being fair means treating all sides equally and justly, without prejudice or favour.

clue.text: Sensational newspaper editor thundered

parts.note: a rag is a disparaging word for a trashy tabloid paper
standard abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: A tabloid boss bellowed at the staff.
explanation.definitionFit: Raged and thundered both mean shouted furiously or stormed with anger.

clue.text: See servant kiss cat

parts.note: a manservant is a man
X is the kiss written at the end of a letter

explanation.surface: An instruction to watch a servant kissing a cat.
explanation.walkthrough: See just tells the solver to look at what follows; it is not the bishop's seat here.
explanation.definitionFit: The Manx is a tailless breed of domestic cat from the Isle of Man.

clue.text: Wise for a second time

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: Someone is told to repeat something, as if a request for an encore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For a second time' reads like 'again', but it splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Sage as an adjective describes someone of profound wisdom and good judgement.

clue.text: Anserine contribution to Christmas chant

parts.note: surface reading: a goose's offering, perhaps its honking voice in a carol
setter's reading: the line about the birds in The Twelve Days of Christmas, the gift on day six

explanation.walkthrough: Anserine means goose-like, from Latin anser; the carol lists gifts for each of twelve days.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the sixth day's gift in the cumulative carol, the one item made of geese.

clue.text: Disorder, so no longer in bed with plonk

parts.note: someone out of bed is up
to plonk something down is to set it down

explanation.surface: Someone has a rough morning after getting out of bed with cheap wine.
explanation.walkthrough: Plonk is British slang for cheap wine, which is the misdirection; here it is the verb meaning put down heavily.
explanation.definitionFit: An upset is a disturbance, as in a stomach upset, so a disorder or derangement.

clue.text: This style of jazz keeps pot alight

parts.note: a dixie is a large metal cooking pot used by soldiers
to alight is to come down and land

explanation.surface: A lively type of music keeps the cooking going on the stove.
explanation.walkthrough: Alight suggests burning, but it is the verb for getting off or coming down.
explanation.definitionFit: Dixieland is early New Orleans jazz, played by small bands with collective improvisation.
